strengths: The construction connects random-forest partitions and ReLU activation regions to local Gaussian density estimates through a common inference framework. This is understandable and potentially useful to researchers studying uncertainty estimation and extrapolation without auxiliary OOD training examples.

The five synthetic geometries allow direct inspection of posterior behavior. Figure 2 reports 45 repetitions with interquartile ranges and provides encouraging evidence of reduced confidence on the sampled OOD region, often with comparable classification accuracy at larger sample sizes.

The human experiment provides a complementary perspective, with 126 retained participants and explicit exclusion criteria. The pseudocode, posterior visualizations, and linked code repository also help readers engage with the proposed approach.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the central uniform-confidence claim. With fixed training data and positive delta, Eqs. (3.6)–(3.8) approach the empirical class priors as the Gaussian densities vanish, rather than 1/K. Thus, an imbalanced training set can produce high majority-class confidence arbitrarily far away. The balanced experiments conceal this discrepancy. Correct the inference rule or explicitly restrict the formulation and claims to equal class priors.

Necessary: Substantiate or remove the consistency assertion in the Introduction. No assumptions or proof establish how partition refinement, neighborhood weights, and covariance estimates yield density consistency as sample size increases. Furthermore, Gaussian decay at infinity does not establish the desired behavior throughout the entire complement of the training-distribution support in Eq. (2.1). Distinguish the demonstrated behavior on distant samples from general OOD guarantees.

Necessary: Reconcile the KDN definition with its pseudocode. Eq. (3.4) compares pre-activation outputs, whereas Algorithm 3, line 12 compares post-activation outputs. These define different weights: with one hidden layer, the first-layer pre-activation is globally affine, so Eq. (3.4) gives zero distance everywhere, while Algorithm 3 generally does not. Identify which estimator generated the results and make the mathematical description consistent with it.

Necessary: Specify the experimental protocol sufficiently to reproduce the findings. The manuscript omits values and selection procedures for C, h, and T; covariance regularization; held-out sample counts and sampling procedures; neural-network training duration; and the OOD detection score. Covariance handling is particularly consequential for sparsely populated polytopes. Also correct the Gaussian XOR specification, which currently assigns identical mixture means to both classes despite the different distributions shown in Figure 1.

Necessary: Qualify the claims of preserving all in-distribution performance and obtaining 'always' better posterior estimates. Figure 2 shows counterexamples: at small sample sizes, Gaussian XOR posterior Hellinger distances are worse for the proposed methods, and KDF has higher classification error on Circle than RF. These learning curves remain informative, but the text should describe the observed tradeoffs and the sample-size regimes where improvements occur.

Necessary: Reconcile the OOD metrics in Table 1. For a ROC point at exactly 95% true-positive rate, a false-positive rate of 0.39 implies AUROC at most 0.9805, whereas KDF on Spiral reports 0.99. This warrants clarification of achieved recall, threshold interpolation, ties, and aggregation, or correction of the reported values. The table also needs uncertainty estimates or an explanation of how results were summarized across repetitions.

Necessary: Narrow or strengthen the human-confidence interpretation. An average class probability near 0.5 can result from opposing confident judgments and therefore does not establish individual uncertainty. Report individual confidence or entropy with appropriate uncertainty estimates, and quantify KDF/KDN agreement under matched conditions if retaining the human-resemblance claim. Otherwise, describe Figure 3 as an exploratory observation about aggregate judgments.

Optional: Compare against ordinary class-conditional KDE or Gaussian mixtures using the same additive bias, and ablate the neighborhood weighting. These comparisons would clarify what the learned partitions contribute. Runtime measurements and higher-dimensional applications would also be useful extensions; a new method, state-of-the-art performance, or large benchmark suite is not required for acceptance of a sound, appropriately scoped simulation study.
